newsitem.title: USA: Firm spending hints job fears fading - Fed sources.
newsitem.headline: Firm spending hints job fears fading - Fed sources.

text.p: U.S. consumers are rushing to the stores and buying with gusto, suggesting that many Americans might have become more confident about their jobs, Federal Reserve sources said.

"For a long time people were somewhat insecure about jobs and now they're feeling a lot better about it; much more willing to go out, go into debt and buy new products," a source at the Federal Reserve told Reuters.

"If they (consumers) were scared about jobs, one would expect them not to be down in the store by this much ... there is some evidence that that uncertainty on the part of households may be fading away," the source added.
The indication is relevant because many economists inside and outside the Federal Reserve believe job insecurity has been one of the main factors preventing wage pressures from increasing sharply.

Any acceleration in wage pressures at this point could easily raise labor costs to companies -- if not matched by increases in productivity -- and as a result trigger upward price pressures at the consumer level, analysts said.
"Clearly, companies are more able and willing to raise prices now than they were perhaps six months ago," the Fed source said.
The indication is relevant as Wall Street debates whether the Federal Reserve will raise short-term interest rates again at the May 20 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committeee (FOMC).
The Fed last raised the federal funds rate on March 25 by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.

The consumer spending/inflation issue has gained even more momentum after some regional Fed presidents recently said consumer spending was strong and that the factors keeping inflation under control could be temporary.

Alfred Broaddus, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, said earlier this month: "My own feeling is that currently most of the risk in the outlook (for 1997) is on the upside ... with the possibility of inflationary pressures.
Broaddus added that most of the factors holding prices and wages down may be "temporary rather than permanent."
The president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Jack Guynn, said earlier this week that consumer spending was a leading force behind the current economic expansion.
"It looks like 1997 is likely to exceed last year's 2.5 percent annualized growth. Where is the strength behind this growth? Consumer spending is leading the way," Guynn said.

Laurence Meyer, a Federal Reserve Board Governor, said this week that aggregate demand in the U.S. economy has been strong, with consumer spending one of the factors contributing to the economic strength.
"The importance is not which component of aggregate demand has been strong, but that aggregate demand (in general) has been strong," Meyer said.
Federal Reserve economists said the current economic situation requires the Fed to be alert and keep a close eye on the inflation ball.

"I don't think that it's true that we're in a situation where you certainly going to see a great surge of inflation," said Brian Motley, research officer and economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.
"But I think we are in a situation where if we're not careful we can see inflation rate gradually creeping up month after month, and I think the Fed is concerned that that not happen," Motley added.
Motley said consumer spending nationwide in the first quarter of 1997 is expected to show a sharp increase over the fourth quarter of 1996.

"The quarter taken as whole, we think it's going to show growth over the fourth quarter of at least five percent, probably six (percent) ... That's a substantial acceleration from last year," Motley said.
The consumer sector accounts for two thirds of the nation's economy.
Analysts said recent data released by the Commerce Department, Conference Board and University of Michigan showed retail sales appear to remain strong, with rising indices of consumer confidence.
